title: Vocal acoustic biomarkers of depression severity and treatment response
finding: In a second study the timing results held: treatment responders paused less and spoke faster. Pitch variability did not show up again.
sample: 105 adults in treatment; 51 responders, 54 non-responders; repeated speech recordings
limit: Recorded speech tasks, not live calls or earbuds; not after TMS.

title: Multilingual markers of depression in remotely collected speech samples: A preliminary analysis
finding: In a large remote cohort, participants with more severe depressive symptoms spoke more slowly and quietly.
sample: 585 participants (RADAR-MDD), speech every two weeks for 18 months
limit: Compares across people, not change within one person; speech tasks on a phone, not conversations.

title: Using speech recognition technology to investigate the association between timing-related speech features and depression severity
finding: Depressed patients had slower speech rate, longer pauses and longer response time than controls; changes in speech rate over time correlated with changes in HAMD-17 score.
sample: 241 people (97 MDD, 68 bipolar, 76 controls), 1,058 recorded interviews with research psychologists, automatic speech recognition
limit: Clinical interviews, not everyday calls; no earbuds; not after TMS.

title: Eavesdropping on happiness: well-being is related to having less small talk and more substantive conversations
finding: The happiest participants spent 25% less time alone (58.6% vs 76.8%) and 70% more time talking (39.7% vs 23.2%) than the unhappiest.
sample: 79 undergraduates wore a recorder (EAR) for 4 days; 30 seconds of sound every 12.5 minutes, coded by people
limit: About well-being in students, not depression; correlational; sound snippets coded by hand, not by a sensor.

title: StudentLife: assessing mental health, academic performance and behavioral trends of college students using smartphones
journal: Proceedings of the 2014 ACM International Joint Conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing (UbiComp)
finding: Over a 10-week term stress rose while positive affect, sleep, conversation and activity dropped off; phone sensor data correlated with mental health outcomes.
sample: 48 students in one class at Dartmouth College, Android phones, 10 weeks
limit: One class of students and correlations only; conversation was sensed by the phone, not earbuds; not patients.

title: Mobile phone sensor correlates of depressive symptom severity in daily-life behavior: an exploratory study
finding: Phone GPS features were related to depressive symptom severity: circadian movement r = -.63, location variance r = -.58; phone usage duration r = .54.
sample: 40 adults recruited, 28 with enough data, 2 weeks, one PHQ-9 at the start
limit: 28 people and one PHQ-9; location and phone use, not conversation or earbuds; the authors say it must be replicated.

title: Talking bodies: nonverbal behavior in the assessment of depression severity
finding: With clinical improvement, behaviours related to negative feelings and social disinterest decreased and pro-social behaviours increased; facial, head and hand movements stood out as indicators.
sample: 40 depressed patients in Brazil, interviews before and after two weeks of tDCS, 21-category ethogram
limit: No healthy control group; behaviour coded by people from interviews; tDCS, not TMS; no earbuds.

title: Loneliness and the onset of new mental health problems in the general population
finding: Adults who were often lonely had higher odds of new-onset depression than those who were not: pooled adjusted odds ratio 2.33 (95% CI 1.62 to 3.34).
sample: Systematic review of 32 longitudinal studies; meta-analysis of 8 independent cohorts
limit: Self-reported loneliness, not measured contact or call time; the authors urge caution because of heterogeneity.

title: Nonverbal social withdrawal in depression: evidence from manual and automatic analysis
finding: Head amplitude and velocity were decreased in high severity interviews.
sample: 19 people, 38 interviews, the same people when severe and when eased; SSRI or psychotherapy
limit: Does not show TMS, daily life, or anything an earbud measured.

title: Facial expression to emotional stimuli in non-psychotic disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Across 39 studies, people with depression showed less facial expression mainly for positive feelings.
sample: 39 studies (abstract only)
limit: Does not show change over time in one person; not earbuds.

title: Music therapy for depression
finding: Music therapy added to usual care beat usual care alone: clinician-rated SMD -0.98 (95% CI -1.69 to -0.27), self-rated SMD -0.85; short-term.
sample: Cochrane review, 9 studies, 421 people with depression
limit: Music therapy with a therapist, small trials, short term only. It is not evidence for playlists or tones in an app.

title: Effects of music therapy on depression: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
finding: Music therapy reduced depressive symptoms (SMD -0.66, 95% CI -0.86 to -0.46), and so did music medicine (SMD -1.33, 95% CI -1.96 to -0.70).
sample: Meta-analysis of 55 RCTs of music-based interventions
limit: Structured interventions in mixed populations, with weaker effects over long periods; does not test self-chosen everyday listening.

title: Music and people with tendencies to depression
finding: Listening to self-selected sad music significantly increased depressed mood in people with high rumination scores, who liked such music all the same.
sample: 175 university students, one self-chosen sad piece on YouTube, mood measured before and after
limit: Students and one listening session; tendency to depression was read from rumination scores, not a diagnosis.

title: Why do depressed people prefer sad music?
finding: People with major depression were more likely to choose sad music, and reported choosing it because it was low in energy, for example relaxing.
sample: 76 women (38 with major depression, 38 healthy controls), two lab music-choice tasks
limit: Women only, lab choices among clips; a group comparison, so it cannot say what one person's playlist means.

title: Global music streaming data reveal diurnal and seasonal patterns of affective preference
finding: Across cultures, people listened to more relaxing music late at night and more energetic music during normal business hours.
sample: 765 million plays streamed by 1 million people in 51 countries
limit: Shows that listening follows time of day and season; it has no mood or depression measure for any listener.

title: Sensorimotor coupling in music and the psychology of the groove
finding: High-groove music elicited spontaneous rhythmic movements, and groove was understood as a pleasurable drive toward action.
sample: Young adults; several studies with ratings, tapping tasks and observed movement
limit: Healthy young adults in a lab; says nothing about depression or what moving less to music would mean.

title: Insomnia as a predictor of depression: a meta-analytic evaluation of longitudinal epidemiological studies
finding: Non-depressed people with insomnia had about twice the risk of developing depression: odds ratio 2.60 (95% CI 1.98 to 3.42) in the random-effects model.
sample: Meta-analysis of 21 longitudinal epidemiological studies
limit: Self-reported insomnia and new depression in the general population; not relapse after treatment, not sensor-measured sleep.

title: Sleep disturbance and depression recurrence in community-dwelling older adults: a prospective study
finding: Among older adults with prior depression, sleep disturbance predicted recurrence independent of other depressive symptoms; 23 (16.9%) had a new episode within two years.
sample: 351 adults aged 60 and over (145 with past depression in full remission, 206 without), 2-year cohort
limit: Older adults and self-reported sleep quality; not after TMS and not a wearable.

title: Relationship between major depression symptom severity and sleep collected using a wristband wearable device: multicenter longitudinal observational study
finding: 14 of 18 Fitbit sleep features were significantly associated with PHQ-8 score, led by awake time percentage, awakenings, insomnia, sleep offset time and hypersomnia.
sample: 368 participants, 2,812 PHQ-8 records, three sites in the Netherlands, Spain and the UK
limit: A wristband, not earbuds; associations varied across sites; an association, not a relapse prediction.

title: The usability of daytime and night-time heart rate dynamics as digital biomarkers of depression severity
finding: Mean heart rate during rest at night was higher in participants with more severe depressive symptoms.
sample: 510 people with a history of recurrent major depression (RADAR-MDD), 6,666 observations over 2 years, wrist-worn Fitbit
limit: Wrist heart rate, not in-ear; an association in a cohort, not a tested early warning.

title: Accurate whole-night sleep monitoring with dry-contact ear-EEG
finding: Automatic sleep scoring from ear-EEG alone reached an average Cohen's kappa of 0.73 against polysomnography.
sample: 20 healthy participants, 80 full-night recordings with polysomnography and dry-contact ear-EEG
limit: Custom ear-EEG electrodes in healthy sleepers. AirPods have no EEG sensor, so this does not apply to them.

title: A meta-analysis of heart rate variability in major depression
finding: Resting heart rate variability is lower in unmedicated depression: RMSSD Hedges' g = -0.462 (95% CI -0.612 to -0.312).
sample: 21 studies, 2,250 patients and 1,982 controls in the whole meta-analysis; RMSSD is the measure with the largest gap
limit: A group difference at rest, not one person over time; not earbuds. AirPods give apps heart rate in bpm, not HRV.

title: Accuracy of heart rate measurement using AirPods Pro 3 during graded treadmill exercise: A laboratory-based validation study
finding: Against a Polar H10 chest strap, mean absolute error was 2.08 bpm overall and 1.31 bpm at rest; limits of agreement -10.27 to 10.22 bpm.
sample: 40 healthy adults (mean age 23.8, 37.5% women), graded treadmill, 16,735 five-second epochs
limit: Does not show heart rate outside a workout, beat-to-beat timing, heart rate variability, or patients on antidepressants.

title: In-Ear PPG for Vital Signs
finding: In-ear PPG was reasonably accurate for vital signs, but absolute error climbed up to 29.84% for heart rate and 24.09% for HRV during motion activities.
sample: Characterisation of a research in-ear PPG across sensor placements and motion artifacts; sample size not given in the abstract
limit: A research sensor, not AirPods; it shows that head and face motion degrade in-ear readings.

title: Activity monitoring in patients with depression: A systematic review
finding: Daytime activity was lower in depression (standardised mean difference -0.76, 95% CI -1.05 to -0.47); during treatment it rose (0.53, 0.20 to 0.87).
sample: 19 papers from 16 studies, 412 patients, wrist sensors
limit: Does not show head motion, earbuds, or relapse. Most studies were not blinded.

title: Embodiment of sadness and depression: gait patterns associated with dysphoric mood
finding: Depressed and sad walkers showed reduced walking speed, arm swing and vertical head movements, more lateral swaying of the upper body and a more slumped posture.
sample: 14 inpatients with major depression against matched never-depressed people; 23 undergraduates with induced mood; motion capture
limit: 14 patients in a lab, a group comparison; not earbud motion and not change within one person.

title: Posture and body image in individuals with major depressive disorder: a controlled study
finding: During depressive episodes patients showed increased head flexion and thoracic kyphosis (both p<0.001); in remission their posture was similar to that of controls.
sample: 34 people with depression and 37 healthy volunteers, posture from digital photos over 10 weeks of drug treatment
limit: Posture from photos in a small study; drug treatment, not TMS; not earbud head pitch.

title: Head pose and movement analysis as an indicator of depression
journal: 2013 Humaine Association Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII)
finding: Depressed people made slower head movements, changed head position less, and spent longer looking down and to the right; 71.2% average recall on unseen people.
sample: 30 people with severe depression and 30 controls, clinical interviews, video
limit: Does not show change within one person. It compares two groups once, on camera.

title: Daily step count and depression in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: In prospective cohorts, people with 7,000 or more steps a day had a lower risk of depression than those with fewer (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.77).
sample: Meta-analysis of 33 observational studies (27 cross-sectional, 6 longitudinal), 96,173 adults
limit: Observational, so it cannot show that walking more prevents depression; general population, not after TMS.

title: Physical activity and incident depression: a meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
finding: People with high levels of physical activity had lower odds of developing depression than those with low levels (adjusted odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.88).
sample: 49 prospective cohort studies, 266,939 people, 1,837,794 person-years
limit: Observational and about new depression in the general population; not relapse and not sensor-measured in most studies.

title: Psychomotor retardation in depression: a systematic review of diagnostic, pathophysiologic, and therapeutic implications
finding: Psychomotor retardation modifies motility, mental activity and speech, and is related to depression severity and therapeutic change.
sample: Systematic review; no pooled estimate
limit: A narrative synthesis without pooled numbers; clinic and lab measures, not earbuds.

title: ExpressEar: sensing fine-grained facial expressions with earables
journal: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies
finding: With a model for each person, 89.9% across 32 posed facial action units; one model for everyone scored 42.1% on people it never saw (chance 3.1%).
sample: 12 people aged 19 to 23 (4 women, 3 of them co-authors), eSense earbuds at 50 Hz
limit: Does not show spontaneous expressions, AirPods, 25 Hz, or anything about mood.

title: Automatic smile and frown recognition with kinetic earables
journal: Proceedings of the 10th Augmented Human International Conference 2019
finding: Seated, F1 0.85 over expressions (smile 0.89); 0.80 for people the model never saw; standing 0.80, walking 0.71.
sample: 9 men in their 20s and 30s, prototype earbud at 130 Hz, each expression cut out with a button press
limit: Does not show talking, natural smiles, or a low sample rate.

title: Hierarchical classification and transfer learning to recognize head gestures and facial expressions using earbuds
journal: Proceedings of the 2021 International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI)
finding: Earbud inertial signals told head from mouth activities with F1 84.79 and nodding from head shaking with 88.24; smile, talk and yawn only 45.42.
sample: Earbud inertial signals during nodding, head shaking, smiling, talking and yawning; sample size not given in the abstract
limit: Abstract only, so sample and sample rate are unknown; smiles were hard to tell from talking; not AirPods.

title: Sensing with earables: a systematic literature review and taxonomy of phenomena
journal: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies
finding: A review of 271 earable publications found 47 different phenomena that can be sensed in, on or around the ear.
sample: Systematic literature review of 271 publications from the ACM and IEEE libraries
limit: A map of what research devices have sensed, mostly in labs; not what AirPods give apps, and nothing about depression.

title: Towards respiration rate monitoring using an in-ear headphone inertial measurement unit
journal: Proceedings of the 1st International Workshop on Earable Computing (EarComp)
finding: Breathing rate from earbud motion was off by 2.62 breaths a minute (accelerometer) and 2.55 (gyroscope), in 20-second windows.
sample: 12 people (2 women), eSense at 50 Hz, nasal cannula reference, keeping still
limit: Does not show AirPods, 25 Hz, walking or talking, or reliable single readings; performance varied drastically between participants.

title: STEAR: robust step counting from earables
journal: Proceedings of the 1st International Workshop on Earable Computing (EarComp)
finding: Earphone motion sensors gave 95% step-count accuracy even in a very slow walk, where smartphone and Fitbit-like systems falter.
sample: Research earphone IMU; workshop paper, sample size not given in the abstract
limit: A workshop paper on research earphones, not AirPods and not patients; a step count is not a mood measure.

title: Introducing AirPods Pro 3, the ultimate audio experience
finding: AirPods Pro 3 have a custom photoplethysmography (PPG) sensor that shines invisible infrared light pulsed at 256 times per second.
sample: Manufacturer announcement; no study
limit: A product statement, not a validation. Apple Support article 123184 documents heart rate for apps during workouts only, and no HRV.

title: A meta-analysis on heart rate variability biofeedback and depressive symptoms
finding: HRV biofeedback lowered depressive symptoms with a medium mean effect size, g = 0.38 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.60; prediction interval -0.19 to 0.96).
sample: Meta-analysis of 14 RCTs, 794 adults; 9 in cardiovascular disease, stress, cancer or alcohol disorder, 5 in non-clinical samples
limit: Few studies were in people with depression as their main diagnosis; programmes of weeks; the prediction interval crosses zero.

title: Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: A meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials
finding: Breathwork lowered depressive symptoms (g = -0.40, 95% CI -0.58 to -0.22) and stress (g = -0.35, 95% CI -0.55 to -0.14).
sample: Meta-analysis of RCTs; depressive symptoms 18 trials; stress 12 trials, 785 adults
limit: Most studies were at moderate risk of bias; mixes slow and fast techniques over weeks; says nothing about one short session.

title: Efficacy of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy in prevention of depressive relapse: an individual patient data meta-analysis from randomized trials
finding: MBCT lowered relapse within 60 weeks: hazard ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.58 to 0.82); 38% relapsed with MBCT, 49% without.
sample: Individual-patient meta-analysis, 9 RCTs, 1,258 people with recurrent depression in full or partial remission
limit: A full manualised MBCT course, not a short exercise in an app; the trials were largely run by proponents of MBCT.

title: Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
finding: Walking or jogging reduced depression against active controls: Hedges' g -0.62 (95% credible interval -0.80 to -0.45).
sample: Network meta-analysis, 218 RCTs, 14,170 people with major depression; walking or jogging n = 1,210
limit: Exercise programmes over weeks, not a walk prompt; confidence was low for walking or jogging; only one study had low risk of bias.

title: Yoga for depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Yoga beat usual care on severity of depression in the short term (SMD -0.69, 95% CI -0.99 to -0.39), rated moderate evidence.
sample: Meta-analysis of 12 RCTs, 619 participants; 3 RCTs had low risk of bias
limit: Short-term only; no long-term meta-analysis was possible and no RCT reported safety data; yoga classes, not a guided audio practice.

title: Behavioural activation for depression; an update of meta-analysis of effectiveness and sub group analysis
finding: Behavioural activation was superior to controls after treatment (SMD -0.74, 95% CI -0.91 to -0.56; 25 comparisons, 1,088 people).
sample: Meta-analysis of 26 RCTs, 1,524 people
limit: Therapist-delivered behavioural activation; study quality was low in most trials and follow-up short.

title: Feasibility and efficacy of the addition of heart rate variability biofeedback to a remote digital health intervention for depression
finding: Response in 56.3% with added HRV biofeedback against 29.2% in historical controls (OR 3.12, 95% CI 1.34 to 7.26).
sample: Not randomised: 48 users of the enhanced programme matched to 48 earlier users; PHQ-9 of 10 or more; 8 weeks
limit: Historical controls and no blinding; most authors worked for Meru Health; it cannot show what the breathing did on its own.

title: Therapist-supported digital mental health intervention for depressive symptoms: A randomized clinical trial
finding: The 12-week programme lowered depression more than a waitlist (d = -0.8); minimal clinically important improvement in 39.1% against 9.8%.
sample: RCT, 100 adults with elevated depressive symptoms; 54 programme, 46 waitlist; 12 weeks
limit: A waitlist control cannot separate the breathing from the therapist, the CBT or the attention; four of seven authors list Meru Health.

title: A therapist-guided smartphone app for major depression in young adults: A randomized clinical trial
finding: The Meru programme plus usual care did not differ significantly from usual care alone on depression at end of treatment or follow-up.
sample: RCT, 124 patients with clinical depression in a Finnish university student health service (72.6% women, mean age 25); 8 weeks, follow-up to 6 months
limit: The primary outcome was null; the gain in patients on antidepressants (d = -0.73) was post hoc and not specified in the protocol.

title: Long-term outcomes of a therapist-supported, smartphone-based intervention for elevated symptoms of depression and anxiety: quasiexperimental, pre-postintervention study
finding: PHQ-9 fell 6.67 points (95% CI 5.59 to 7.75) and the change held at 12 months.
sample: One group before and after, 102 adults, no control group, no HRV biofeedback yet
limit: With no control group the fall cannot be credited to the programme; Meru authors.

title: Effectiveness of 2 just-in-time adaptive interventions for reducing stress and stabilizing cardiac autonomic function: microrandomized trials
finding: Stress and rumination fell after every 1-minute exercise irrespective of the kind of prompt and intervention; mindful breathing was no better than looking at an object.
sample: Two preregistered micro-randomised trials, 60 and 50 young adults, 4 days, exercises triggered by a wearable at low HRV
limit: Healthy students over 4 days; the authors cannot rule out order effects; not depression.

title: Efficacy of contextually tailored suggestions for physical activity: a micro-randomized optimization trial of HeartSteps
finding: A walk prompt raised steps in the next 30 minutes by 14% on average (p = .06); the effect was no longer distinguishable from zero by day 28.
sample: Micro-randomised trial, 44 adults, 6 weeks, up to 5 randomised prompts a day
limit: Steps, not mood, in healthy adults; it warns that daily prompts wear off.

title: Just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs) in mobile health: key components and design principles for ongoing health behavior support
finding: Defines the JITAI as support of the right type and amount at the right time, and notes many were developed with minimal empirical evidence or theory.
sample: Framework paper with examples; no new data
limit: A design framework, not evidence that any just-in-time intervention works.

title: Remote Assessment of Disease and Relapse in Major Depressive Disorder (RADAR-MDD): recruitment, retention, and data availability in a longitudinal remote measurement study
finding: Remote measurement in people with a history of depression was feasible: 80% completion of primary outcome assessments; 110 participants had over 50% of data across all data types.
sample: 623 people with a history of major depressive disorder; longitudinal remote measurement study
limit: Shows feasibility and data availability, not that sensors predict relapse.

title: Relapse prediction in schizophrenia through digital phenotyping: a pilot study
finding: The rate of behavioural anomalies in passive phone data in the 2 weeks before relapse was 71% higher than during other periods.
sample: 17 patients with schizophrenia, Beiwe app on their own phones for up to 3 months; pilot
limit: Schizophrenia, not depression; 17 people; phone data, not earbuds.

title: The accuracy of passive phone sensors in predicting daily mood
finding: One model for the whole sample did poorly (median R² about 0); personal models beat chance for 75 of 93 people (80.6%).
sample: 271 Android users in a remote depression trial (BRIGHTEN), daily PHQ-2; 93 had enough data for a personal model
limit: Does not show future days: the personal models used random splits, not time order. Phone use, not motion.

title: The efficacy of measurement-based care for depressive disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
finding: Measurement-based care gave greater remission (OR 1.83, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.97; 5 studies) but no significant difference in response (OR 1.66, 95% CI 0.66 to 4.17).
sample: Meta-analysis of RCTs in adults with depressive disorders treated with pharmacotherapy
limit: Rating scales during drug treatment, not sensors; few trials with high risk of bias; not relapse and not TMS.

title: Mood Monitoring, Mood Tracking, and Ambulatory Assessment Interventions in Depression and Bipolar Disorder: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
finding: The review found an absence of evidence on the effect of mood monitoring on decreased relapse rates or readmission rates.
sample: Systematic review, 8 RCTs, 1,230 participants
limit: Does not show that monitoring fails. It shows no trial has proven it works for relapse.

title: Durability of antidepressant response to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation: systematic review and meta-analysis
finding: Among initial responders, 66.5% sustained response at 3 months, 52.9% at 6 months and 46.3% at 12 months.
sample: Meta-analysis of 19 studies; the 12-month figure rests on 9 studies, 247 patients
limit: Mostly open follow-ups; it says how often benefit fades, not how to see it coming.

title: Durability of clinical benefit with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in the treatment of pharmacoresistant major depression: assessment of relapse during a 6-month, multisite, open-label study
finding: 38 of 99 (38.4%) had symptoms worsen within 24 weeks; 32 of those 38 (84.2%) regained benefit when TMS was reintroduced.
sample: 99 people on one maintenance antidepressant, open-label, 24 weeks
limit: Open label with no control group; worsening was caught by a clinician's rating two weeks running, not by a sensor.

title: Can medication free, treatment-resistant, depressed patients who initially respond to TMS be maintained off medications? A prospective, 12-month multisite randomized pilot study
finding: One TMS session a month did not differ significantly from watching and re-treating; 78% and 63% responded to reintroduction.
sample: Randomised open-label pilot, 49 people off antidepressants, 12 months; 16 completed all 53 weeks
limit: A small open pilot; it does not show which schedule or trigger is best.

title: Systematic review of preservation TMS that includes continuation, maintenance, relapse-prevention, and rescue TMS
finding: Across 30 sources and 1,494 people, the quality of evidence for efficacy of preservation TMS was rated low; support was clear but mostly uncontrolled.
sample: Systematic review: 4 randomised trials (1 sham-controlled), 14 open trials, 12 case series
limit: Protocols vary widely; there is no randomised test of reintroducing TMS early against late.
